en: Mayon volcano's perfect cone makes it prone to pyroclastic flows, so staying outside the six-kilometer Permanent Danger Zone saves lives.
Living near the Philippine Trench means coastal residents must immediately walk to higher ground when a strong earthquake shakes the ground.
The Sierra Madre mountain range acts as a natural barrier that protects Metro Manila from the strongest typhoons coming from the Pacific.
The heavily polluted Pasig River contains dangerous bacteria and toxic waste, so children should never swim in it to avoid severe waterborne infections.
The tropical climate of the Philippines allows mosquitoes to breed year-round, making daily removal of stagnant water essential to prevent dengue fever.
Mount Pulag's peak reaches nearly 3,000 meters, so hikers must wear thick jackets to avoid hypothermia from the dangerously freezing mountain temperatures.
The Philippines is located near the equator, so wearing sunscreen and hats during outdoor activities prevents severe sunburns and dangerous heatstroke.
The Chico River in the Cordillera region relies on healthy mountain forests to filter rainwater and provide safe drinking water for local communities.
Swimming near the coral reefs of Tubbataha requires wearing water shoes to protect your feet from sharp rocks and venomous sea urchins.
Lake Lanao in Mindanao provides hydroelectric power, but residents must avoid dumping garbage into it to prevent severe water contamination and dangerous flooding.
When Taal Volcano erupts, wearing N95 masks protects your lungs from inhaling harmful volcanic ash that can cause serious breathing problems.
The Philippine Valley Fault System runs through highly populated areas, so building earthquake-resistant houses prevents tragic injuries during strong ground tremors.
